Latin Squares

AlgorithmsCountingInvariants
Game: Put numbers in a grid so each appears once per row and column — and maybe symmetrically too.
How to play: Click two cells in a row to swap them, or use the arrows to cycle a row. Restore resets the grid.
Look for the math

A grid where every row and column has each number once is surprisingly easy to build — even with the symmetry rule.

The cyclic construction

Put (i + j) mod n + 1 in row i, column j (starting from zero). Every row is a shift of every other, so each number occurs once per row and once per column. Because i + j = j + i, the grid is also symmetric about the main diagonal — solving the applet's harder problem at the same time.

Why the moves break it

Cycling one row keeps its own numbers distinct but repeats values in the columns. Swapping two different cells in a row breaks the row's distinctness. The logic test checks the construction for every size from 2 to 9, rejects grids with repeated row or column entries, and confirms the effects of both moves.

Swap two cells, then repair the square using only row cycles and swaps. How many moves do you need?
